name: Felix Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing biomedical science, so it's chemistry labs on Tuesdays, a lot of cell biology, and a stats module that's honestly the best thing I've done. I live in a flat share with a guy who does physics and a girl who does art, and I work evenings at a climbing gym, running the front desk and doing the booking system. Dad drives a delivery van and pays about half my costs, and I cover the rest. I use AI for everything, summarising papers, quizzing me before exams, fixing my code for the stats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, because I'd say I think that's wrong but fine. I'd tell my friends the tools are already useful, and if the progress stalls it's still a free tutor. But I'd say don't confuse a calm year with a calm decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it would be a bit of a letdown. I'm betting some of my career on tools getting better, and the lab jobs I want are competitive because the field's small. If nothing changes, I'm just a normal graduate in a normal queue for lab posts with average grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and push my skills. I'd learn Python properly, since lab data work is where the jobs are, and I'd email a lecturer about summer lab placements. I'd keep the climbing gym job because the booking system is a good bit of real software experience. And I'd put 30 a week away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty fine. Slightly restless, because I like change and this is the boring timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money's the only real squeeze. Dad's van needs a new gearbox soon, and that's a bill he'd have to find. If he cut my share, I'd add two evenings at the gym and probably drop to five hours of study a week, which my grades can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a lab at nine in the morning with a pipette, running samples and writing up results with an AI helping. I want to work on cancer diagnostics. With average grades I won't get the top PhD, but a technician or analyst route is realistic, and I'm okay with that.

say: I'd tell friends the tools are already a free **tutor**, even if progress stalls.
I'd say a calm year isn't a calm **decade**.
think: This is the **boring** timeline, and I'm betting some of my career on better tools.
With average grades I'd aim for **technician** or analyst lab roles.
do: Learn **Python** properly for lab data work.
Email a lecturer about summer lab **placements**.
Save **30 a week** and keep the gym job.
feel: **Fine**, a bit restless, because I like change.
S0.quote: Don't confuse a calm year with a calm decade.
fieldNote: Felix is mildly **disappointed** by a no-change world.
His money worry is concrete: his dad's **van** and a gearbox bill.
He sees his gym booking system as **real experience**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one that actually matches what I see. Writing, checking, coding, it's already happening in my own study. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now because the people who use them well will have more doors open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's good for me. A lot of lab work is thinking work on top of the hands-on: planning experiments, analysing data, reading papers. Tools do the first draft of all of it. The risk is junior roles disappearing because one analyst with a tool does what three used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper. I'd build a small data project in my second year, like analysing a public cancer dataset, so there's something real to show. I'd teach my flatmates. I'd also keep the lab placement plan and start a side project selling booking-system setups to other gyms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a bit of nerves. I like being early, but I'm aware I don't have a safety net if I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym front desk goes first. The booking and payment parts are almost automatic already, and the owner would love to cut staff hours. It's four of us now and I'd say two within a year. That's about 12 hours of my wage, which is real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it changes how I study. I'd focus on how to check what a tool says, because lab results that look right and are wrong cost real money. I'd choose modules on statistics and bioinformatics over pure memorising, because memorising is what tools do better than me.

I'd say this timeline matches what I already see in **study**.

Junior roles could vanish if one **analyst** can do the work of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if it's real, we're about to find out what we are for. I'd also say to every friend: don't sit it out. I'd post about it online and argue with people saying it's all hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be rattled. Thinking work is most of what I want to do. If AGI does analysis better than any graduate by 2028, the lab analyst job I want could be gone before I qualify in 2029. Hands-on lab work would last till about 2031, but it's a thin lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on being useful right now. I'd get every skill I can with the tools, start the booking-system side business properly, and try to land a hands-on lab placement this summer, since that's the part robots take last. I'd also talk to Dad about not spending his savings on my degree if the degree stops making sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and wired at the same time. I like the pace, but I know I'd lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but food and rent. I'd go to five gym evenings and use the quiet hours to build things. I'd ask a lecturer, honestly, whether a three-year degree is the right move or whether I should switch to something more hands-on, like a lab technician apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on myself first, then on a few friends who are into the same stuff. I'd lean on Dad for a bed if things collapsed. I'd lean on the university careers office a bit, but I'd bet they're as lost as anyone.

say: I'd say we're about to find out what we are **for**.
I'd tell every friend not to **sit it out**.
think: If analysis goes first, the **lab analyst** job I want could vanish before I qualify.

do: Land a hands-on lab **placement** this summer.

feel: **Scared** and wired at once, and I'd lose sleep.
S2.quote: Hands-on lab work would last till about 2031, but it's a thin lifeline.
fieldNote: Felix's **adaptability** shows as action, not panic.
He considers an **apprenticeship** over the degree.
His fear is about **thinking-work** jobs vanishing before he qualifies in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the version where people who prepare win. I'd tell friends to use the five years to build skills nobody can copy cheaply, like working with people and judging results. And I'd say I'd rather be early than right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be nervous but mostly excited. I'd graduate in 2029 into a world two years from AGI, and that's weird, but there would still be hands-on work till around 2034. I'd be on the edge of it, and I like that more than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, spend the summers in labs, and keep building small data projects. I'd get comfortable with every tool for research, and I'd save about 60 a week from the gym and the side jobs. I'd keep my eyes on companies working on lab automation. Someone will need to run the lab automation machines, and I'd rather be that person than the one who gets replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a good way. It's the kind of nerves you get before a big match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year one, I'd finish the degree first. I'd also have time to get a proper lab placement and see what hiring really looks like in 2028. In the short version I might drop out of my course. Here I'd probably stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide in second year, once I see how labs and hospitals are actually hiring. If junior analyst roles are already drying up, I'd head for the hands-on lab and automation side. If they aren't, I'd stay on the science route and try for a master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is real time, so use it. I'd tell people not to get complacent, and I'd say now is the cheapest time ever to learn almost anything with a tool. I'd keep posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. By 2036 I'd be 29 and about seven years into a lab career, and hands-on robots come 2039. I'd have time to build a reputation. I'd worry a bit about what the economy looks like, but I'm betting my adaptability is an advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a master's in bioinformatics, and work in a lab. I'd keep the side business, because it's a way to learn how to sell. I'd also try to buy a small flat with a friend. And I'd keep learning every new tool as it comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. This is the one I'd pick if I could choose. I'd feel like I'm riding it instead of being hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I can build a career and a second skill, and maybe start a small company. With two years I'm just reacting. Time is what turns luck into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend to go for it, but to pick a version of the degree that has maths and data in it. I'd say learn the tools in first year, not final year. A degree is still useful as long as you treat it as a starting point, not a ticket.

I'd tell people ten years is real time, so **use it**.

My **adaptability** is an advantage, but I can't predict the economy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. Everything that makes my path attractive, like analysis and thinking, is exactly what falls first, and I'd have no time to build a second skill. What would help is a way to retrain quickly, funded, with real hands-on options, and honest advice from universities.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't scared of the tools, we're scared of being late. I'd like more people to tell us what's actually coming, instead of what's comfortable.

headlineQuote: People my age aren't scared of the tools, we're scared of being late.
portrait: Felix is a **biomedical science** first-year, 19, in a flat share, with his dad's van income behind him.
He works at a **climbing gym** desk and uses AI every day for study.
He is progressive and adaptive, and treats tools as an **advantage** and a way to move first.
He wants a **lab** career in cancer diagnostics and plans a technician or analyst route.
He is calm in slower worlds and anxious when AGI arrives in **two years**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because thinking work would fall first and he'd have no time for a second skill.
whatWouldHelp: Funded, fast **retraining** with hands-on options, plus honest advice from the university.
